topics.topic: Whether accepted no-op owner actions write audit entries under A14 required test 7
questions: Must an accepted owner action that changes nothing write an audit entry, or must test 7 be limited to accepted actions that change state and the exceptional erasure of old entries?
Must this say that the accepted action writes an entry only when it changes state, except that erasing old entries always writes one, so that accepted no-op actions remain covered by rules 1 and 3?
Does an accepted owner action listed by M09 write its mapped audit entry only when it changes state, or even when it is an accepted no-op?

quotes:
An accepted action that changes nothing (A03 rule 4, A05) writes no entry,
   but for the erasure of old audit entries (A15 rule 6).

The imported `OWNER_AUDIT_ACTIONS` constant has exactly one row for each
   owner action M09 lists, for each customer mark transition and each
   project erasure kind, the erasure of old entries among them, and no other
   row; and each such action, accepted, writes the audit action its row
   names (rule 1).
judgement.divergence: For an accepted repeat archive that changes nothing, rule 3 leaves the audit log unchanged while Required test 7 requires the mapped archive entry; the owner reading the log observes the difference.
judgement.why: The unconditional accepted-action clause in Required test 7 requires an entry for an accepted no-op, while A14 rule 3 forbids that entry except for erasing old audit entries.
options: Qualify Required test 7 with the changed-state condition and the erasure-of-old-entries exception.
Require every accepted listed owner action, including no-ops, to write an entry and revise A14 rules 1 and 3 and the conflicting tests.
consequences: The first option preserves the accepted rule that the audit log records state changes; the second changes the audit guarantee and causes accepted no-ops to add entries.

topics.topic: Whether the A21 security review must acknowledge A13's confirmation-digest collision exception
questions: Must the security review say that test 12 shows refusal only when the changed tuple does not share the bound digest, as test 12 itself says, or is collision refusal intended to remain guaranteed?
Does “changing any of them is refused” exclude a different encoding whose digest collides with the bound digest, as A13 rule 6 and test 12 do, or does A21 assert refusal even for that case?
Is A21 claiming exact confirmation binding even for two encodings that share a digest, or must this security-review conclusion carry A13's new collision exception?

quotes:
its
   inputs — for the import, the file's digest
   and the picks — kept as a digest of those values in a fixed order, never
   as the values themselves; a submission's inputs are bound when their digest
   equals it. The digest is a collision-resistant cryptographic digest of one
   unambiguous encoding of the action, the target, the version and the inputs
   in that order, every list in its order and an absent value told apart from
   an empty one, so that two different tuples never share an encoding; that
   two encodings share a digest is outside the guarantee.

A13 rule 6 states what the digest of a
confirmation's inputs guarantees — one unambiguous encoding of the action,
target, version and inputs under a collision-resistant cryptographic
digest, a collision of that digest outside the guarantee — and test 12
shows that changing any of them is refused.

Reviewed
under authentication_credential_abuse and authorization (A09: the same
rights and classes, read from the release), browser_boundary and
concurrency (A13: a confirmation binds what its step showed, no more),
secrets and concurrency (A14: the same entries in the same transactions)
and files_artifacts (A22: the same one declared type): no right, limit,
class or answer moved, and no outcome changed.
judgement.divergence: For distinct confirmation tuples with the same digest, A13 treats the submitted inputs as bound and places the collision outside its refusal guarantee, while A21 says every changed component is refused and that the confirmation binds only what the step showed; the owner observes admission versus refusal.
judgement.why: A21 claims exact binding and refusal for every changed value, but A13 expressly defines binding by digest equality and excludes collisions from the guarantee.
options: Qualify A21's test and security-review conclusions with A13's digest-collision exception.
Remove A13's exception and require confirmation binding that refuses distinct colliding tuples.
consequences: The first option aligns the security review with the accepted digest-based guarantee; the second strengthens the product guarantee and requires changing the binding rule.

topics.topic: Whether A16 exact import mapping must reject or prevent applying a different tuple with a colliding confirmation digest
questions: When two different bound input tuples share the confirmation digest, is the later tuple allowed because A13 places the collision outside its guarantee, or must A16 still guarantee that only the tuple shown by the step can be applied?

When a submitted import tuple has a different unambiguous encoding but the same confirmation digest, must the import still apply only the tuple shown by the confirmation step, or is that collision outside A16's exact-mapping guarantee as A13 now states?

quotes:
a submission's inputs are bound when their digest
   equals it. The digest is a collision-resistant cryptographic digest of one
   unambiguous encoding of the action, the target, the version and the inputs
   in that order, every list in its order and an absent value told apart from
   an empty one, so that two different tuples never share an encoding; that
   two encodings share a digest is outside the guarantee.

The owner confirms that mapping in the confirmation
   step (A13 rule 6); the confirmation applies the file of that digest, the
   picks, names, aliases and Customer values the mapping showed, nothing
   else; a file no longer kept is refused and must be uploaded again.

The file and the
   picks are bound by their digest, the names, aliases and Customer values
   with them, so the mapping it builds is the one the step showed but for
   the ids production gained in between; every such id is one Registry
   mints at random (Identity formats; M01, M03, M05), the import — the one
   path for an id from outside — being closed after its one success
   (rule 8).
judgement.divergence: For a submitted import tuple Y distinct from the shown tuple X but sharing its confirmation digest, A13 treats Y as bound, while A16 requires the confirmation to apply only X's shown file and values; the owner and later store readers observe which tuple is imported or whether the action is refused.
judgement.why: A13 permits a colliding tuple to satisfy the binding check, while A16 unconditionally guarantees that the applied mapping contains only the tuple shown by the confirmation step.
options: Exclude confirmation-digest collisions from A16's exact-mapping guarantee.
Keep A16's unconditional exact-mapping guarantee and strengthen the binding rule so distinct colliding tuples cannot be applied.
consequences: The first option narrows the import guarantee consistently with A13; the second preserves exact preview-to-commit identity but changes the accepted confirmation guarantee.

author_guidance: Before editing, identify the decision's owning state from the phase purpose, question_scope and layer obligations, then choose a disposition for each topic that awaits one.
fixed: repair a decision the owning state must make; do not add later-layer implementation choices merely to close a topic. Record the fix commit and review the changed text once.

carried: name the receiving layer and use --what to preserve the choice, its options and consequences, and the required guarantee every option must keep. Decide any guarantee owned here before carrying its execution onward.
accepted: explain why the remaining choice is permitted. Bring an unresolved product choice to the owner with its options and consequences; absence of a quoted requirement does not decide it.
contradiction and standard_violation take no disposition: repair the offending text in its owning state and review the change. Deterministic transition findings must also close through their checks.
State 2: decide required results and constraints, including necessary refusal precedence; carry test mechanisms, exact contracts and deployment procedures to their owners.
